title: Dynamical Steering and Unambiguous Signature of Majorana Corner Modes in Altermagnetic Josephson Junctions
abstract: Dynamical manipulation of Majorana zero modes and their unambiguous distinction from topologically trivial states remain paramount challenges in topological quantum computation. Here, we propose a phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junction as a versatile platform for generating and controlling Majorana corner configurations. Moving beyond conventional global parameter tuning that merely toggles the topological phase in situ, our platform utilizes the macroscopic superconducting phase difference and the Néel-vector orientation as independent control knobs to dynamically reshape the boundary mass. This synergistically enables the deterministic spatial relocation of Majorana corner modes (MCMs) among selected corners of a fixed device geometry. Crucially, this spatial reconfiguration yields a definitive experimental fingerprint: a control-correlated conductance switching. As the MCMs are relocated, the quantized zero-bias peak perfectly emerges at the target corner while simultaneously vanishing at the initial one. This macroscopically phase-locked spatial correlation effectively eliminates false positives from trivial Andreev bound states, establishing a control-correlated diagnostic and a promising route toward future Majorana braiding architectures.
summary: The paper proposes using phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a highly controllable platform for generating and manipulating Majorana Corner Modes. By independently tuning the superconducting phase difference and the magnetic order vector, researchers can deterministically move these topological states across a fixed device geometry. The definitive proof of this control is achieved by observing a unique conductance switching signature that confirms the physical relocation of the zero-energy modes.
main_problem: The research addresses two major hurdles in topological quantum computation: deterministically moving Majorana Corner Modes (MCMs) and providing an unambiguous diagnostic to distinguish true MCMs from trivial bound states.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that by controlling the superconducting phase difference ($\phi$) and the altermagnetic Néel-vector orientation ($\mathbf{n}$), they can deterministically steer MCMs between corners, evidenced by a unique control-correlated conductance switching signature.
method: Theoretical analysis involving solving boundary conditions on a lattice model, utilizing symmetry protection (e.g., time-reversal and particle-hole symmetry at $\phi=\pi$), and projecting the altermagnetic perturbation onto the edge Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The platform is a phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junction realized in a superconducting system exhibiting helical Topological Superconducting (TSC) phases. The physics is governed by coupling between superconductivity, Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and the magnetic order parameter ($\mathbf{n}$).
key_observables: Zero-bias conductance peak ($G(0)$), which must switch location precisely when MCMs are relocated; the boundary mass term $m_\vartheta$.
important_parameters: Superconducting phase difference ($\phi$), Néel vector orientation ($\mathbf{n}$), and the superconducting gap parameters ($\Delta_1, \Delta_{-1}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes $\mu=0$ for specific gap closing conditions; it relies on continuum limit approximations and lattice regularization techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing MCM localization regimes (I-VI), the spatial mapping of boundary mass terms ($m_\vartheta$), and local tunneling spectroscopy confirming the zero-bias conductance switching during mode relocation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, derives the low-energy edge Hamiltonian using symmetry protection, analyzes how external parameters ($\phi$ and $\mathbf{n}$) modulate the effective boundary mass term ($m_\vartheta$), and finally presents the diagnostic signature via local tunneling conductance measurements.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the engineering challenges of topological quantum computation by providing a physical mechanism (altermagnetism) to control Majorana modes spatially, which is crucial for building braiding architectures.

Regions I–VI denote distinct MCM corner-localization regimes; brown and gray regions indicate gapless and trivial regimes, respectively. (c) Corner-localization patterns of the MCMs for the six regions labeled in (b). Colored dots mark the corners occupied by MCMs. (d) Local tunneling readout of the zero-bias conductance near a contacted corner.

FIG. 3. Control and phase robustness of MCMs. (a) Proba- bility density of the zero-energy modes at ϕ = π and n ∥[1¯1]. (b) Finite-size spectrum versus ϕ, demonstrating the persis- tence of the zero-energy modes over a finite phase interval. (c),(d) Probability density and corresponding finite-size spec- trum away from the π-junction limit at φ = 0.35π, showing relocated MCMs isolated within the quasiparticle gap.

FIG. 2. Boundary spectra and real-space distributions for different N´eel vector orientations. (a),(b) For n ∥ˆz, the cylinder spectrum hosts gapless helical Majorana edge modes, whose lowest-energy states extend along the boundaries in a fully finite geometry. (c),(d) For n ∥[11], the altermagnetic spin splitting gaps the boundary modes and produces zero- energy modes localized at the corners. The insets in (b) and (d) show the corresponding finite-size spectra.
